passages.happening:
The book opens with a narrator setting the scene. “These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel in the wilderness east of the Jordan” (verse 1). The time is exact: ‘In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month’ (verse 3). Israel has just defeated two kings, Sihon and Og (verse 4). “On the east side of the Jordan in the land of Moab, Moses began to explain this law” (verse 5).

Between the place and the date sits one short remark. It takes eleven days to go from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea (verse 2).

Then Moses speaks. He begins his story at Horeb, where God said to Israel, “You have stayed at this mountain long enough” (verse 6). They were to go up and take the land. “See, I have placed the land before you. Enter and possess the land that the LORD swore He would give to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The first five verses are not Moses' own words. Someone else is introducing him, the way a person introduces a speaker. After that, almost the whole book is Moses' voice.

Horeb is the name Deuteronomy usually gives to Mount Sinai. It is where God made his covenant with Israel and gave the Ten Commandments.

The people listening are the children of those who left Egypt. Their parents refused to enter the land and died in the wilderness. Now this generation is camped across the river from it. Before Moses gives them the law again, he tells them how they came to be standing here.

Verse 2 is easy to pass over, and it carries the weight of the chapter. The road from Horeb to the edge of the land was eleven days long. Verse 3 says it is now the fortieth year. The contrast is deliberate. Eleven days became forty years, and Moses is about to explain why.

Several of the place names in verse 1 are unknown today. Scholars are not sure whether they mark the spot where Moses spoke or recall stages of the wilderness years.

The word translated ‘explain’ in verse 5 tells a reader what kind of book this is. Moses is not only repeating laws. He is making them plain, the way a teacher or a preacher does.

Notice how God's command ends. The land is the one ‘the LORD swore He would give to your fathers’. Israel is not being sent to seize something. It is being sent to receive what was promised to Abraham centuries before.
passages.later:
The promise Moses names goes back to the first book of the Bible. God told Abraham, “To your descendants I have given this land” (Genesis 15:18).

Numbers ends where this book begins: “These are the commandments and ordinances that the LORD gave the Israelites through Moses on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho” (Numbers 36:13).
passages.asks: Moses starts with memory before he gives a single command. Ask how well you know the story of how you came to where you are, and what God has done in it. And notice the eleven days. Ask whether there is ground you have been circling for years that God placed in front of you long ago.

passages.t: Sharing the load: leaders and judges
passages.happening:
Moses remembers how the people grew too many for one man to lead. “I cannot carry the burden for you alone” (verse 9). God had made them ‘as numerous as the stars in the sky’ (verse 10), and Moses prays for a thousand times more (verse 11). “But how can I bear your troubles, burdens, and disputes all by myself?” (verse 12).

So the tribes chose wise and respected men, and Moses appointed them as leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (verses 13-15).

He gave the judges their charge. “Hear the disputes between your brothers, and judge fairly between a man and his brother or a foreign resident. Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike. Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God” (verses 16-17). Cases too hard for them were to come to Moses.
passages.hearers:
Exodus 18 tells how this system began, on the advice of Moses' father-in-law, Jethro. Here Moses tells it without Jethro, and stresses that the people agreed: “What you propose to do is good” (verse 14). Dividing a people into thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens was a common way to organize them, both for war and for settling disputes.

The reason Moses gives for the change is a happy one. The people have multiplied ‘as the stars in the sky’. That is the wording of God's promise to Abraham, who was told to look up and count the stars. Moses' burden is the weight of a promise being kept.

The charge to the judges would have sounded sharp in the ancient world. A judge who took bribes or bent toward the powerful was a familiar evil. Israel's judges are told to hear ‘small and great alike’. The poor man's case gets the same hearing as the rich man's.

The ‘foreign resident’ of verse 16 was a non-Israelite living among the people. He had no land and no clan to stand up for him. The law names him so that he will not be the one person the court forgets.

The reason for all of it is in six words: ‘for judgment belongs to God’. A judge in Israel does not own the verdict. He is handling something that belongs to someone else, and he will answer for it.

The Hebrew verb for ‘judge’ means more than handing down a ruling. It means setting things right.
passages.later:
Moses first received this plan from Jethro: “Furthermore, select capable men from among the people” (Exodus 18:21).

King Jehoshaphat gave his judges the same reason centuries later: “Consider carefully what you do, for you are not judging for man, but for the LORD” (2 Chronicles 19:6).

The letter of James carries the rule against partiality into the church: “My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism” (James 2:1).
passages.asks: Moses admits he cannot carry the people alone. Ask what you are carrying alone that was never meant for one person. And think of the people whose case you hear, at work, at home or in church. Ask whether the small and the great get the same hearing from you.

passages.t: Kadesh: ‘you were unwilling to go up’
passages.happening:
Israel crossed ‘the vast and terrifying wilderness’ and reached Kadesh-barnea, at the edge of the land (verse 19). Moses said, “Go up and take possession of it as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not be afraid or discouraged” (verse 21).

The people asked to send men ahead to look over the land. Moses agreed and chose twelve (verses 22-23). They came back carrying fruit and said, “It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us” (verse 25).

“But you were unwilling to go up; you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God” (verse 26). The people grumbled in their tents: ‘Because the LORD hates us, He has brought us out of the land of Egypt’ (verse 27). The cities were too strong and the people too tall.

Moses pleaded with them. God would fight for them as he had in Egypt, and in the wilderness, ‘where the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son’ (verse 31). “But in spite of all this, you did not trust the LORD your God” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The fuller story is in Numbers 13 and 14. Moses retells it as a preacher, with his eye on the people in front of him.

He says ‘you’: ‘you were unwilling’, ‘you grumbled’. Most of the men who refused at Kadesh are dead. Moses is speaking to their children. He speaks as if they had been there, because they now stand where their parents stood, at the edge of the land, facing the same choice. Every later reader is drawn into the story in the same way.

There is a difference from Numbers. There God tells Moses to send the scouts. Here the people propose it and Moses agrees. Many readers hold that both are true, and that Deuteronomy is stressing the people's own part.

What the people say in their tents is the darkest sentence in the chapter: ‘the LORD hates us’. They had been rescued from slavery, fed every day and led by fire and cloud. They looked at all of it and decided it was a plot to kill them. Fear had rewritten their whole history.

Their description of the cities, ‘with walls up to the heavens’, is the language of dread. It is exaggeration, though Canaanite cities did have strong walls and ramparts. The Anakim were a people remembered for their great size.

Moses answers the lie with a picture. God has carried Israel ‘as a man carries his son’. The Hebrew verb for ‘carry’ is the same one Moses used of himself in verse 9, when he said he could not carry the people alone. What Moses could not do, God had been doing all along.

Verse 32 names the failure. The word for ‘trust’ is the word used of Abraham, who believed the LORD. It means to treat someone as firm. The word ‘amen’ comes from the same root. Israel's problem at Kadesh was not that it counted the enemy wrongly. It would not lean on God.
passages.later:
The prophet Hosea heard God speak of Israel with the same tenderness: “It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them in My arms” (Hosea 11:3).

Isaiah carries the picture through a whole lifetime: “I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you” (Isaiah 46:4).

The letter to the Hebrews looks back on Kadesh and names the same cause Moses names: “So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter” (Hebrews 3:19). That warning is written to the church about its own heart. It is not a charge against the Jewish people.
passages.asks: Israel said, ‘the LORD hates us’, with manna on the ground outside the tent. Ask whether fear has ever made you read your own story that way, as if God meant you harm. Then set Moses' picture beside it. Ask where, looking back, you can see that you were carried.

passages.t: The oath, and the battle God did not send
passages.happening:
God heard the people's words and swore an oath. “Not one of the men of this evil generation shall see the good land I swore to give your fathers, except Caleb son of Jephunneh” (verses 35-36). Caleb would enter ‘because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly’.

Moses adds, “The LORD was also angry with me on your account, and He said, ‘Not even you shall enter the land’” (verse 37). Joshua would lead Israel in. And the children the people had said would be taken captive ‘will enter the land that I will give them, and they will possess it’ (verse 39).

The people then changed their minds. “We have sinned against the LORD,” they said. “We will go up and fight” (verse 41). God said, ‘Tell them not to go up and fight, for I am not with you’ (verse 42). They went anyway. The Amorites ‘chased you like a swarm of bees’ (verse 44). The people came back and wept, and God would not listen. So they stayed at Kadesh a very long time.
passages.hearers:
The oath answers the people's words. They had said their little ones would be carried off. God says those little ones will have the land. The people standing in front of Moses as he speaks are those children. They are the proof that God kept the second half of the oath.

Then comes a second rebellion, and it looks like the opposite of the first. First the people would not go when God said go. Now they go when God says stay. Moses uses the same Hebrew word for both: ‘you rebelled’ (verses 26 and 43). The fault was not fear of fighting, since the second time they were eager to fight. In both cases they did what they had decided for themselves.

Their confession, ‘We have sinned’, sounds right. But they do not wait to hear what God says next. They treat being sorry as if it undid the sentence, and they march out to prove it. Verse 41 says they thought it would be easy.

‘I am not with you’ is the heart of God's warning. Israel's strength was never its weapons. Without God the same hill country that was promised to them became the place of their defeat.

The chapter ends heavily. The people weep, God does not listen, and the camp sits at Kadesh while the years begin to pass.
passages.later:
Numbers records the people's own words, which God turns around here: “Our wives and children will become plunder” (Numbers 14:3).

Psalm 95 turned this oath into a call for every later generation of worshipers: ‘Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts’ (Psalm 95:7-8).

The letter to the Hebrews takes up that psalm and says the offer is still open: “Therefore, while the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it” (Hebrews 4:1).
passages.hard:
Moses says God was angry with him ‘on your account’. Numbers says Moses was kept out of the land for his own failure. Which is it?

Numbers 20:12 gives the reason in God's words: “Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them.” That was at the waters of Meribah, years after Kadesh, when Moses struck the rock.

Readers have explained the difference in several ways.

Many see no contradiction. Moses failed at Meribah when the people's quarreling pressed him. Both things are true. Numbers stresses what Moses did, and Deuteronomy stresses the people's part. Deuteronomy itself names Moses' own fault later in the book: ‘both of you broke faith with Me’ (32:51).

Others think Deuteronomy shows Moses sharing the fate of the people he led. He bears the result of their rebellion along with them.

Critical scholars often see two old accounts of why Moses did not enter the land, kept side by side.

These notes do not settle it. What a reader can see is that Moses does not hide the matter. He tells the new generation, in his first speech, that he too is shut out. He brings it up again in chapters 3 and 4, and it is plainly a grief to him. The note on chapter 3 says more.
passages.asks: The people were sorry, and then marched off to fix things in their own strength. Ask whether you have ever treated an apology as a way to escape what your choices set in motion. And take the warning of verse 42 to heart. Before the next thing you rush to do for God, ask whether he sent you.
